doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: After the Army: school, race, politics
title: FAMU's rejection and color lines among Black Americans
summary: Fuller says FAMU refused him over his parentage and the GI Bill, and talks about lighter complexions in politics and Hollywood, from Obama to Belafonte and Poitier.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: It doesn’t work because “Who are your parents?” “My parents are deceased.” “How are you going to pay for this education?” “G.I. Bill.” “Oh we don’t accept G.I. Bill here.” If your father, Dr. Brown, was some sort of light-skinned…
So, you’re talking about the—When you say the lighter, the brighter, the better. You see, browns stick around, and if your light your alright. If your brown stick around, if you’re black, get back.

I could put it simple for you; let’s start with Harlem. The first black congressman that came into power, you’re damn near his complexion. There was Charlie Rangel right behind him. Ernest Morill, the senator from…
Brooks, then the other guy from Tennessee.
Obama! Now, if he had been my complexion, he wouldn’t have been even thought about. It’s still like the old days. Nina Horn as opposed to… Harry

Belafonte as opposed to Sidney Poitier. Who is a better actor than Sidney Poitier? And, before him, what was his name that did the whiteface thing? One of the first actors played with Charles Laughton and all those people. I’m having a senior moment right now.
